tagline: Two lanes through the Green Mountains, then east along the Ottauquechee.
intro: East of Rutland, US 4 winds through the Green Mountains as a two-lane highway, passing Mendon and Killington before following the Ottauquechee River valley. Vermont Tourism includes the Crossroad of Vermont in its scenic-byway collection: a 50-mile east-west route from Rutland to the New Hampshire border, including Killington and Woodstock. At Sherburne Pass, the crossing lies between Pico Peak and Deer Leap Mountain; farther east, Quechee Gorge drops 165 feet beneath the surrounding land.

The road through Rutland and Woodstock to White River Junction became Route 13 in the New England road marking system in 1922, then US 4 in late 1926. West of Rutland, a 19-mile expressway was built for a proposed East–West Highway that never materialized. Its final eastern segment opened in 1986, and the old surface route there became US 4 Business.

Eastward from Rutland, US 4 passes Mendon and Killington, then follows the Ottauquechee through Bridgewater and Woodstock. Beyond Taftsville, it reaches Quechee Gorge and turns toward the White River. At Quechee, the highway bridge itself offers a view into the gorge. It follows that river into White River Junction before crossing the Connecticut River into New Hampshire on the Lyman Bridge.

moments.title: Sherburne Pass
moments.text: Pico Peak stands south of Sherburne Pass, with Deer Leap Mountain to the north. The pass divides two drainage systems: eastward water reaches the Ottauquechee and Connecticut rivers, then Long Island Sound. Westward water reaches Lake Champlain and eventually the Saint Lawrence. The Appalachian and Long trails once crossed Route 4 at the height of the pass. Both moved to Pico’s west slope; their former route is now the blue-blazed Sherburne Pass Trail. The western ascent begins in Mendon, while the height of land lies within Killington, with the east side draining through Kent Brook and the west through Mendon Brook.
moments.notice: From the pass, Pico Peak’s summit has the shape of a cone.

moments.title: Taftsville Covered Bridge
moments.text: The village’s mills had created the need for a river crossing. Stephen Taft and his brother established them within a decade of his arrival in the early 1790s. Three bridges at this Ottauquechee crossing fell to floods, in 1807, 1811 and 1828. Solomon Emmons III was then contracted to build a more resilient crossing, completing the timber-framed covered bridge in 1836. That bridge survives. Hurricane Irene badly damaged it in 2011, and it reopened in September 2013 after two years of repairs. Its two spans meet at a central pier in the river gorge.

moments.title: Quechee Gorge
moments.text: Quechee Gorge is Vermont’s deepest gorge, a 165-foot cut along US 4. The Ottauquechee runs along its bottom. The gorge formed approximately 13,000 years ago as the Laurentide Ice Sheet withdrew. Its carving is thought to have followed the draining of glacial Lake Hitchcock, when the Ottauquechee rapidly cut downward. The cut exposes bedrock of the Devonian Gile Mountain Formation, with Mesozoic mafic dikes visible on the west wall.
moments.notice: The gorge is visible from the US 4 bridge and trails on both sides.
